result:
The proposed answer of 1/4 is wrong, because both halves of the argument fail.

**Lemma 1 is false.** A square adjacent to two holes uses two different edges of that square, for example its east and west edges. These edges are disjoint, so the hole boundaries need not intersect. The upper bound h ≤ n/4 therefore has no valid basis.

**The construction is also invalid.** In the proposed plus-shaped arrangement, the squares at (3i+1, 3j+1) are not in P. Each hole touches such a square diagonally at a corner, and that square is connected to the outside region. So each hole's boundary meets the outer boundary at a corner point, which violates the condition.

**A better construction gives density 1/3.** Put single-square holes at (2i, 2j) and let P be all other squares in a large block, that is, every square with at least one odd coordinate. Two holes are never edge-adjacent or corner-adjacent, so their boundaries are disjoint. P is connected. Each hole accounts for 3 squares of P, so h/n tends to 1/3, which exceeds 1/4. Boundary effects vanish as n grows. Along the block's edges one can keep a ring of P so that no hole touches the outer boundary.

Hence the limit is at least 1/3, so 1/4 cannot be correct.

VERDICT: REJECT
